overview: This file consists of a three-page despatch from the American Consulate General in Hong Kong reporting the opening of the Japanese Domei News Agency’s first regular local office for selling its news service. It identifies the office’s manager, Robert Y. Horiguchi, describes its small client base and unsuccessful approaches to Chinese newspapers, and argues that the venture was intended primarily to disseminate Japanese-favorable accounts of the Sino-Japanese War rather than to make a profit. The despatch also records a rumor that the Hong Kong Press had accepted German and Japanese subsidies and notes signs of increasingly pro-German coverage.

people.name: Robert Y. Horiguchi
people.role: Manager of the Domei News Agency office in Hong Kong; formerly a journalism student at the University of Missouri and an employee of the Hearst International News Service in Chicago

people.name: Addison E. Southard

subfiles.title: Despatch on the opening of the Domei News Agency office in Hong Kong
subfiles.from: Addison E. Southard, American Consul General in Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Reports on the establishment, personnel, customers, and apparent propaganda purpose of the Domei News Agency’s new Hong Kong office.
subfiles.summary: Southard reports that Domei opened a regular Hong Kong office on May 1, 1938, under Robert Y. Horiguchi, a former University of Missouri journalism student and Hearst International News Service employee. The office had secured only three local clients, while none of the more than twenty Chinese newspapers approached had subscribed, and the Hong Kong Government closely controlled its incoming radio news. Southard concludes that the commercially unpromising office was established to circulate Japanese-colored war news and counter coverage criticized by Japanese newspapers. He also records a rumor that the Hong Kong Press had accepted subsidies from Germany and Japan, although its coverage appeared more clearly Germanophile than pro-Japanese.

interest: The despatch offers a compact contemporary account of Japanese overseas news operations during the Sino-Japanese War, including Domei’s business model, staffing choices, customers, and relations with colonial controls. It is particularly useful for its candid assessment that the Hong Kong office was politically rather than commercially motivated and for its characterization of Horiguchi’s education, employment history, and perceived suitability as a propagandist. The unverified report of German and Japanese subsidies to the Hong Kong Press also illustrates American diplomatic concern about coordinated foreign influence over the colonial press.
